questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $K=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$. Which argument proves that $\lambda\boldsymbol{x}\in K$ for every $\boldsymbol{x}\in K$ and every $\lambda\geq0$?
options: Each row gives $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}(\lambda\boldsymbol{x})\leq\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq0$, because multiplying by $\lambda\geq0$ cannot increase a number.
$\boldsymbol{A}(\lambda\boldsymbol{x})=\lambda\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}$ holds for every real $\lambda$, so $\lambda\boldsymbol{x}\in K$ for all real $\lambda$ and $K$ is a subspace.
$\boldsymbol{A}(\lambda\boldsymbol{x})=\lambda\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}$, and multiplying a vector with all entries $\leq0$ by $\lambda\geq0$ keeps every entry $\leq0$.
$\boldsymbol{0}\in K$ and $K$ is convex, so $\lambda\boldsymbol{x}=\lambda\boldsymbol{x}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{0}$ lies in $K$ as a convex combination.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ have nonzero rows $\boldsymbol{a}_1^{\top},\dots,\boldsymbol{a}_m^{\top}$. Which geometric description fits the polyhedral convex cone $K=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$?
options: The intersection of $m$ closed halfspaces whose boundary hyperplanes all pass through the origin.
The union of $m$ closed halfspaces whose boundary hyperplanes all pass through the origin.
The intersection of $m$ open halfspaces whose boundary hyperplanes all pass through the origin.
The intersection of $m$ closed halfspaces that each contain the origin in their interior.

questions.question: Let $K_1=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}_1\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and $K_2=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}_2\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}_1\in\mathbb{R}^{m_1\times n}$ and $\boldsymbol{A}_2\in\mathbb{R}^{m_2\times n}$. Which description of $K_1\cap K_2$ is correct for every such pair?
options: $K_1\cap K_2=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon(\boldsymbol{A}_1+\boldsymbol{A}_2)\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ when $m_1=m_2$, by adding the two systems row by row.
$K_1\cap K_2$ is a convex cone, but in general not a polyhedral one, because the walls of $K_1$ and $K_2$ cut each other.
$K_1\cap K_2$ is a polyhedral convex cone only when all rows of $\boldsymbol{A}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{A}_2$ together are linearly independent.
$K_1\cap K_2=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, where $\boldsymbol{A}$ has the rows of $\boldsymbol{A}_1$ followed by those of $\boldsymbol{A}_2$.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^n$, how is the family of polyhedral convex cones $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ related to the family of finitely generated convex cones $\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_k\})$?
options: Every finitely generated convex cone is polyhedral, but some polyhedral convex cones need infinitely many generators.
The two families are equal: every polyhedral convex cone is finitely generated, and every finitely generated one is polyhedral.
Every polyhedral convex cone is finitely generated, but some finitely generated convex cones need infinitely many walls.
The families agree in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where each wall carries a generator, but they differ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n\geq3$.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$ be nonempty and $K=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, with the same matrix $\boldsymbol{A}$. For $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$ and $\boldsymbol{d}\in K$, which statement is guaranteed?
options: The whole line $\{\boldsymbol{x}+t\boldsymbol{d}\colon t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ through $\boldsymbol{x}$ lies in $V$.
The half-line $\{t\boldsymbol{d}\colon t\geq0\}$ starting at the origin lies in $V$.
The half-line $\{\boldsymbol{x}+t\boldsymbol{d}\colon t\geq0\}$ starting at $\boldsymbol{x}$ lies in $V$.
The point $\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{d}$ lies in the cone $K$ as well.

questions.question: Let $K=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&-2\\-1&0&3\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following points lies in $K$?

The set $K=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1\geq2x_2,\ x_2\geq0\}$ is to be written as $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$. Which matrix $\boldsymbol{A}$ does this?
options: $\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-2\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$
$\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1-2x_2\leq2,\ x_1\geq0,\ x_2\geq0\}$, the feasible region of a linear program, written as $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$. Which set is the cone $K=\{\boldsymbol{d}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{d}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ with the same matrix $\boldsymbol{A}$?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{d}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon d_1-2d_2\leq0,\ d_1\geq0,\ d_2\geq0\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{d}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon d_1\geq0,\ d_2\geq0\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{d}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon d_1-2d_2\leq0\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{d}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon d_1-2d_2\geq0,\ d_1\geq0,\ d_2\geq0\}$

questions.question: Which of the following subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a polyhedral convex cone, that is, equal to $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ for some real matrix $\boldsymbol{A}$ with two columns?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon |x_1|\geq|x_2|\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon |x_1-x_2|<x_2\}\cup\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon |x_1-x_2|\leq x_2\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon |x_1-x_2|\leq x_2+1\}$

questions.question: For $c\in\mathbb{R}$ let $K_c=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+cx_2\leq0,\ -x_1\leq0,\ -x_2\leq0\}$. For which values of $c$ is $K_c=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$?
options: For every $c\geq0$.
For every $c>0$.
For every $c<0$.
For no value of $c$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $K=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$. Exactly when is $K=\mathbb{R}^n$?
options: When every row of $\boldsymbol{A}$ is the zero vector.
When the rank of $\boldsymbol{A}$ is smaller than $n$.
When $\boldsymbol{A}$ has fewer rows than columns, $m<n$.
When the rows of $\boldsymbol{A}$ add up to the zero vector.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $K=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$. Which set equals $K\cap(-K)=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{x}\in K\text{ and }-\boldsymbol{x}\in K\}$ for every such $\boldsymbol{A}$?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$ only, since a polyhedral convex cone never contains a whole line.
$K$ itself, since a convex cone is closed under multiplication by $-1$.
The row space of $\boldsymbol{A}$, the span of its rows $\boldsymbol{a}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{a}_m$.
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\}$, the null space of $\boldsymbol{A}$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}$ be a nonzero row of $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $K=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$. Which statement about the vector $\boldsymbol{a}$ holds for every such $\boldsymbol{A}$?
options: $\boldsymbol{a}\in K$, because the rows of $\boldsymbol{A}$ are generators of the cone $K$.
$\boldsymbol{a}$ points to the side of the wall $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=0$ that contains no point of $K$.
$-\boldsymbol{a}\in K$, because $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}(-\boldsymbol{a})=-\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{a}<0$.
$\boldsymbol{a}$ lies on its own wall, that is, $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{a}=0$.

questions.question: The set $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+2x_2\geq4,\ x_1\geq0,\ x_2\geq0\}$ equals $K+Q$, where $K$ is the nonnegative quadrant and $Q$ is the segment from $(4,0)$ to $(0,2)$. Which statement about writing $\boldsymbol{p}=(5,1)$ as $\boldsymbol{q}+\boldsymbol{d}$ with $\boldsymbol{q}\in Q$ and $\boldsymbol{d}\in K$ is correct?
options: It is possible in exactly one way, namely $\boldsymbol{q}=\tfrac{4}{7}\boldsymbol{p}$ and $\boldsymbol{d}=\tfrac{3}{7}\boldsymbol{p}$.
It is possible for every $\boldsymbol{q}\in Q$, by taking $\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{p}-\boldsymbol{q}$.
It is possible in more than one way, for example $(4,0)+(1,1)$ and $(2,1)+(3,0)$.
No such decomposition exists, since $\boldsymbol{p}$ is not a convex combination of $(4,0)$ and $(0,2)$.

questions.question: Which system of inequalities describes the half-line $H=\{t(1,2)\colon t\geq0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ in the form $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$?
Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon -x_1\leq0,\ x_1-x_2\leq0,\ -x_2\leq1\}$, a polyhedral convex set whose right-hand side is $(0,0,1)$. Which statement about $V$ is correct?
options: $V$ is a polyhedral convex cone, because its third inequality follows from the first two.
$V$ is not a cone, because its right-hand side $(0,0,1)$ is not the zero vector.
$V$ is not a cone, because $(1,1)\in V$ but $-(1,1)=(-1,-1)\notin V$.
$V$ is a cone, but its cone $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ is strictly smaller than $V$.

questions.question: Let $L=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_1^2+x_2^2\leq x_3^2,\ x_3\geq0\}$, which is a closed convex cone. Is $L$ a polyhedral convex cone?
options: Yes: $L$ is described by $x_1^2+x_2^2-x_3^2\leq0$ with right-hand side $0$, which is what makes a set polyhedral.
No: putting $x_3=1$ into finitely many inequalities $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq0$ cannot cut out the unit disc in $x_1,x_2$.
Yes: $L$ is the intersection of the halfspaces through $\boldsymbol{0}$ bounded by its tangent planes, each of the form $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq0$.
Yes: $L$ is a closed convex cone, so by the Minkowski–Weyl theorem it is finitely generated and hence polyhedral.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^m$, $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$ and $K=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{0}\}$. Suppose only that $K\neq\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$. What can be concluded about $V$?
options: $V$ is unbounded.
$V$ is empty or contains a whole line through each of its points.
$V$ is empty or unbounded.
$V$ is empty or contains every point of $K$.

questions.question: Let $K=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1-3x_2\leq0,\ -x_1-x_2\leq0\}$. By the Minkowski–Weyl theorem $K$ is a finitely generated convex cone. Which pair of vectors satisfies $K=\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2\})$?
options: $\boldsymbol{v}_1=(1,-3)$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(-1,-1)$
$\boldsymbol{v}_1=(-3,-1)$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(1,-1)$
$\boldsymbol{v}_1=(3,1)$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(1,-1)$
$\boldsymbol{v}_1=(3,1)$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(-1,1)$

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1-x_2\leq2,\ -x_1+3x_2\leq3\}$, which contains $\boldsymbol{0}$. For which objective vector $\boldsymbol{c}$ is the linear program $\max\ \boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$ unbounded?
options: $\boldsymbol{c}=(-1,2)$
$\boldsymbol{c}=(-1,3)$
$\boldsymbol{c}=(1,1)$
$\boldsymbol{c}=(1,-1)$
